clue.text: What many would rather have than distemper?

definitions.text: What many would rather have than distemper?

parts.words: What many would rather have than distemper?
parts.note: distemper is both a dog disease and an old water-based paint for walls, so the clue asks what decorators prefer to paint as a covering

explanation.surface: A wry question about which ailment, or which pet trouble, people would sooner put up with.
explanation.walkthrough: Distemper reads as the canine illness, but it is also a cheap wall paint; the preferred alternative wall covering is the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Decorative paper pasted on walls is the usual rival to painted distemper as an interior finish.

clue.text: 'e pads about and proceeds with difficulty

indicators.note: about means the letters are scattered around into a new order

parts.note: the printed words give E, P, A, D, S; the setter needed WADS, so the fodder is E plus WADS

explanation.surface: A cockney figure shuffles around, making slow, laborious progress.
explanation.walkthrough: As printed, 'pads' gives a P the answer lacks; the setter or typesetter must have meant 'wads', and 'about' then rearranges E and WADS.
explanation.definitionFit: To wade is to walk through water or mud, so it means moving forward laboriously.

clue.text: A bit of bacon fat with nothing on

parts.note: lard is pig fat
nothing is zero, the letter O
taken as written

explanation.surface: A rasher of bacon that is pure fat with nothing more added.
explanation.walkthrough: A lardoon (lardon) is a strip of bacon fat threaded through lean meat in cooking.
explanation.definitionFit: A lardoon is a small strip of pork fat or bacon used for larding meat.

clue.text: Grand arrays to criticize — nothing works

parts.note: to pan a show is to criticize it harshly
nothing is zero, the letter O
plies means works at, as in plying a trade

explanation.surface: Someone finds fault with impressive displays and concludes none of it is effective.
explanation.definitionFit: A panoply is a splendid full display or array, originally a complete suit of armour.

clue.text: Opening peril — army in a mess

indicators.note: being in a mess means being jumbled up, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A dangerous start to a campaign, with the troops in disarray.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' looks like part of the phrase 'in a mess', but it is fodder; 'a mess' alone rearranges PERIL, ARMY and IN.
explanation.definitionFit: Something preliminary is introductory, coming at the start before the main business.

clue.text: Untrained when hostilities arise

indicators.note: in a down clue, rising means the word is read from the bottom upwards

parts.note: hostilities between nations make a war

explanation.surface: Green recruits sent in when fighting breaks out.
explanation.definitionFit: Raw recruits are inexperienced, new and not yet trained.

clue.text: Waugh's success in journalism

definitions.meaning: Evelyn Waugh wrote a comic novel about Fleet Street with this title
an exclusive story published ahead of rival papers

explanation.surface: Praise for a writer's triumph in the newspaper world.
explanation.walkthrough: Waugh's 1938 novel satirises newspaper reporting, so both senses sit on the same subject.
explanation.definitionFit: An exclusive news story beats rival papers, and Waugh's satirical novel takes that word as its title.

clue.text: Society joined by self-righteous moralist as a young man

parts.note: a prig is a smug, self-righteous person

explanation.surface: A club admits a sanctimonious member when he was still a youth.
explanation.definitionFit: A dated term for a youth or young fellow, likened to a small shoot of a plant.

clue.text: Sanctimonious, in the head's view

indicators.note: in means one piece sits inside the other

parts.note: onion is old slang for the head
pi is short for pious, meaning sanctimonious

explanation.surface: In the headmaster's opinion, a pupil is being sanctimonious.
explanation.walkthrough: 'onion' for the head is slang, as in 'off one's onion'.
explanation.definitionFit: A view is a personal belief or judgement on a matter.

clue.text: Exclusively RAF officers admitted, by design

indicators.note: admitted means let in, so one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: purely means solely or exclusively
POs are Pilot Officers in the Royal Air Force

explanation.surface: Only air-force officers were let in, and that was deliberate.
explanation.definitionFit: Doing something on purpose means doing it deliberately, intentionally.

clue.text: Put out of order — badly angered

indicators.note: badly signals that the letters of the next word are messed up

explanation.surface: A furious person has disrupted everything.
explanation.definitionFit: To derange is to throw into disorder or disarray.

clue.text: Wordsworth's happy character or Cowper's queen

definitions.meaning: Wordsworth's poem 'Character of the Happy ...' describes the ideal fighting man
Cowper's poem 'Boadicea' celebrates the British fighting queen of the Iceni

explanation.surface: A literary quiz about a figure from two English poems.
explanation.definitionFit: Both poets portray a fighter: Wordsworth's ideal soldier and Cowper's battling queen Boadicea.

clue.text: Condescend to bribe all round

indicators.note: all round means the bribe surrounds the other word

parts.note: a sop is something given to pacify, a bribe
taken as written

explanation.surface: Lowering oneself to pay someone off to get one's way.
explanation.definitionFit: To stoop is to lower oneself morally, to deign to do something beneath one.

clue.text: In a bit of machinery, wandering into the unknown

parts.note: taken as written
a cog is a toothed part of a machine

indicators.note: wandering means the letters of into stray into a new order

explanation.surface: Inside a piece of machinery, something drifts off into uncharted territory.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wandering' rearranges INTO to make NITO after IN and COG.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone travelling in disguise or under an assumed name goes unrecognised.

clue.text: Game that might take one to Paris?

definitions.meaning: a card game, a form of baccarat

definitions.text: that might take one to Paris?
definitions.meaning: in French the phrase means railway, which could carry a traveller to the French capital

explanation.surface: A pastime that could transport you to France.
explanation.walkthrough: The game's French name literally means 'road of iron', the railway.
explanation.definitionFit: The baccarat variant is named with the French phrase for railway, which might carry a traveller to Paris.

clue.text: Married an employee

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A domestic servant has wed.
explanation.definitionFit: A male servant or worker is called a man, as in 'my man' for a valet.

clue.text: Nobody to play one so good?

definitions.text: Nobody to play one so good?

parts.words: Nobody to play one so good?
parts.note: read as a word for someone so skilled that no opponent can give them a game, without any contest

explanation.surface: A player so outstanding that nobody will take them on.
explanation.walkthrough: The word for peerless is read literally as 'without a match', with no game to play.
explanation.definitionFit: Unrivalled or peerless: so good there is no equal, read cryptically as having no game against anyone.

clue.text: Varied eastern scenic ride of colourful quality

indicators.note: varied means altered, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: An oriental tourist trip through scenery noted for its vivid hues.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Varied' rearranges E, SCENIC and RIDE together.
explanation.definitionFit: Iridescence is a shimmering play of rainbow colours, as on a soap bubble.

clue.text: Steer, obstinate, is -badly shaken

parts.note: to con a ship is to direct its steering
cussed means stubborn, obstinate

explanation.surface: A stubborn young bullock has been badly rattled.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Steer' looks like a young bullock, but it is the verb: to con is a nautical word for directing a ship's course.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone concussed has had the brain jolted by a blow, a violent shaking.

clue.text: interpretation of a high church movement

definitions.meaning: rendering a text in another language
the transfer of a bishop from one see to another, or of a saint's relics

explanation.surface: Explaining a reform movement within the Anglo-Catholic church.
explanation.walkthrough: 'high church' suggests a religious party; here it means moving a senior churchman such as a bishop to another diocese.
explanation.definitionFit: Rendering words in another language, and in church usage the moving of a bishop or relics to a new place.

clue.text: Lover — married, unhappily

indicators.note: unhappily signals the letters are disturbed into a new order

explanation.surface: A suitor whose marriage is not a happy one.
explanation.definitionFit: An admirer is a suitor, someone romantically attracted to another.

clue.text: Bark — at anchor here perhaps?

definitions.meaning: a wide inlet of the coast where ships may lie at anchor

explanation.surface: A ship called a bark lies moored in some sheltered water.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bark' looks like a sailing vessel, which fits the anchor, but it is the dog's cry.
explanation.definitionFit: A hound's howl, and a broad coastal inlet where vessels moor.

clue.text: Perhaps it's able to describe Beauty's 18

indicators.note: perhaps suggests a possible rearrangement of the letters

explanation.surface: A word that might fit Beauty's suitor in the fairy tale.
explanation.walkthrough: 18 is ADMIRER; Beauty's admirer is the Beast in 'Beauty and the Beast', so the adjective fits him.
explanation.definitionFit: Beastly or animal-like, which suits the Beast who courts Beauty.

clue.text: Serpentine type of wood-nymph

definitions.meaning: the king cobra, a large venomous snake
in Greek myth a nymph living in and dying with a tree

explanation.surface: A snake-like kind of forest spirit.
explanation.definitionFit: Both a tree spirit of Greek myth and the king cobra of India.

clue.text: Thing known as a starting point

definitions.meaning: a fact given or known, from which inferences are drawn
a fixed reference level from which measurements begin

explanation.surface: Something established as the place to begin.
explanation.definitionFit: A given fact, and a fixed reference level from which measurements start.

clue.text: Disturb — with a surprising result

definitions.meaning: an unexpected win by an underdog

explanation.surface: Unsettle things by producing an unexpected outcome.
explanation.definitionFit: To disturb or unsettle, and an unexpected victory by an outsider in sport.

clue.text: Sweet little daughter of the cloth

parts.note: twee means cutesy, excessively sweet
D is the short form of daughter

explanation.surface: A charming little girl born of a clergy family.
explanation.walkthrough: 'of the cloth' suggests the clergy, but cloth is simply the fabric.
explanation.definitionFit: A rough woollen fabric, originally from Scotland.

clue.text: Stray cat — one, maybe — not certain

parts.note: to err is to stray from the right path

indicators.note: maybe suggests the letters could be put in some other order

parts.note: one is the Roman numeral I

explanation.surface: A wandering feline, possibly one of several, of uncertain whereabouts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'maybe' rearranges CAT and I to make ATIC after ERR.
explanation.definitionFit: Erratic means irregular and unpredictable, so its behaviour is uncertain.

clue.text: Lettuce is about — bigger than usual

parts.note: C is short for circa, Latin for about
OS is the abbreviation for outsize

explanation.surface: A lettuce that has grown larger than normal.
explanation.definitionFit: A long-leaved variety of lettuce, the romaine.

clue.text: Jovial one, against being taken in by Will's fool

indicators.note: being taken in means held inside the other piece

parts.note: Feste is the jester in Shakespeare's Twelfth Night
one is the Roman numeral I
V is short for versus, against

explanation.surface: A cheerful person, opposed to being fooled by Shakespeare's clown.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Will' is William Shakespeare; his fool Feste holds I and V.
explanation.definitionFit: Festive means merry and celebratory, in a holiday mood.

clue.text: Second to prepare for exam? Be off with you!

parts.note: to cram is to study intensively for a test

explanation.surface: A student revising is told by someone to get lost.
explanation.definitionFit: An informal command to go away at once.

clue.text: Dropped bombs fore and aft — by the way, coloured red

parts.note: ST is the abbreviation for street, a way
raddled means daubed with raddle, red ochre

explanation.surface: Bombers hit both ends of a red-painted vessel along a road.
explanation.walkthrough: To straddle a target is to drop bombs on either side of it.
explanation.definitionFit: In bombing or gunnery, straddling a target means landing shots on both sides of it.
